question: arXiv:2610.26648v1 studies cascade annihilation of dark matter through on-shell scalar mediators, χχ → φφ, with the mass ratio r = m_φ/m_χ. In the 4τ channel, how does the dark matter mass preferred by the Galactic Center excess change as r is lowered from 1, and which kinematic explanation does the paper suggest for the change of direction? Give the relation it states for the value of r at which the τ-energy range is widest, and the value of r it quotes for m_χ ≃ 15 GeV.
reference_answer: As r is reduced, the mass preferred by the excess first decreases, down to r ≈ 0.5, and then increases again at smaller r; at intermediate r the mediated cascade prefers smaller masses than the effective χχ → 4τ benchmark. The first shift toward smaller masses is consistent with the change of the photon spectrum caused by the mediator boost. The change of direction may be related to the competition between the mediator boost and the finite τ mass: for a scalar mediator the τ energy is uniformly distributed between E± = (m_χ/2)[1 ± √(1−r²)·√(1−4m_τ²/(r²m_χ²))], and at fixed m_χ this range is widest at r = √(2m_τ/m_χ), which is r ≃ 0.49 for m_χ ≃ 15 GeV, close to the value at which the preferred region turns toward larger masses. The paper offers this as a possible, qualitative explanation, because the photon spectrum also depends on the subsequent τ decays.

question: arXiv:2610.26648v1 repeats its Galactic Center fit with FRONT+BACK events instead of the FRONT-only events of the main analysis. Between which values does the ratio of the FRONT+BACK to the FRONT excess intensity lie above 0.78 GeV, by how much is the FRONT+BACK intensity lower in the four lowest-energy bins, and why does the paper say that this low-energy offset is more significant than the quoted deviations suggest?
reference_answer: For diffuse-emission Model X, above 0.78 GeV the ratio lies between 0.92 and 1.06 in all bins, within about 1σ, and its weighted mean over the 14 common bins is 1.00. In the four lowest-energy bins (0.275–0.784 GeV) the FRONT+BACK intensity is lower by 9–18%; each bin deviates by less than 2σ (at most 1.7σ), but all four in the same direction. Because the FRONT events are a subset of the FRONT+BACK sample, the two spectra are positively correlated and the uncertainties of the ratio, which were added in quadrature, are overestimated; the offset is therefore more significant than these numbers suggest.

question: In arXiv:2112.09706v2, the Galactic diffuse emission models differ in the assumed magnetic field, interstellar radiation field and gas, which changes how the inverse-Compton templates evolve with energy. According to the paper, how much does the morphology of the inverse-Compton templates change between 1 GeV and 10 GeV — in which sky regions and for which models are the two extremes it quotes — and, after the fitting procedure, at what level do the composite count maps predicted by different diffuse models still differ?
reference_answer: Comparing the inverse-Compton emission at 10 GeV with that at 1 GeV, the paper finds that the shape of the templates changes by no more than a few per cent in the regions of the Fermi Bubbles (the case it quotes is Model I) and by more than 40% along the Galactic disk (the case it quotes is Model XV). After the fit, the composite count maps predicted by different diffuse models (summed over all template components) still differ at the O(10%) level; the paper shows this for 1.02–2.24 GeV, each model against Model I.

question: arXiv:2209.00006v2 compares the best-fit spectra of its Galactic Center excess candidates when each is fitted together with ring-based templates. Which candidate gives the faintest excess, and how good is its fit? What does the paper say about the spectra of the candidates that include the boxy bulge? And how does the dark matter spectrum obtained with the ring-based templates compare with those spectra and with the dark matter result obtained with the astrophysics-based templates of Cholis et al.?
reference_answer: The X-shaped bulge yields the faintest excess and is also the worst-fitting candidate. Every candidate that contains the boxy bulge (alone, with the nuclear stellar bulge added, or varying together with the X-shaped bulge) ends up with nearly the same spectrum, a comparatively soft one, which the authors read as the template having absorbed diffuse flux that the model lacks. The dark matter spectrum obtained with ring-based templates is on average harder than those; in shape it resembles the dark matter result found with the astrophysics-based templates, but its flux is lower, and it has bin-to-bin “wiggles” that neither dark matter annihilation nor millisecond pulsars would produce.

question: arXiv:1005.5480v3 tests the uniformity of the Fermi bubble spectrum by splitting the bubble template into a north and a south bubble, and it also repeats the template fit with the Haslam 408 MHz map in place of the simple disk model as the inverse-Compton template. In the north–south split of the fit that uses the simple disk model as the inverse-Compton template, which of the two bubbles comes out with the slightly harder spectrum, and to what does the paper attribute this? Why is the Haslam map not an ideal tracer of the inverse-Compton emission, and how does the fitted bubble spectrum change when it is used?
reference_answer: In the fit with the simple disk model, the northern bubble comes out slightly harder than the southern one. The authors put this down to Loop I: its template, whose spectrum is softer, is fitted only in the northern sky. Either bubble is still harder than all the other fitted components, and the overall conclusion stays that the bubbles are north–south symmetric and spectrally uniform. As for the Haslam 408 MHz map, it shows the bright Loop I structure and mostly traces synchrotron radiation of softer electrons (around 1 GeV), whereas inverse-Compton emission is set by the electron distribution together with the interstellar radiation field. When it is used, the bubble spectrum is still the hardest component, but its correlation coefficients are raised at low energies, below about 2 GeV.

question: In arXiv:1511.08787v2, how do the antiproton bounds on dark matter annihilating into b quarks through multi-step cascades change when the number of cascade steps is increased, and what reason does the paper give? reference_answer: More cascade steps make the antiproton bounds tighter once the dark matter is heavier than about 20 GeV. question: arXiv:1410.3696v1 derives the isotropic diffuse gamma-ray background with three reference foreground models, A, B and C. Why do the authors go beyond the class of Galactic diffuse emission models studied before, to which model A belongs, and in what do models B and C differ from model A?
reference_answer: Model A belongs to the previously studied class, which assumes one diffusion coefficient for the whole Galaxy and a single source population for electrons and nuclei (following the pulsar distribution). With models of that class the inverse-Compton template does not behave consistently in the multi-component fit: the fitted inverse-Compton spectrum differs from the one the model predicts. If the cause is a wrong sky distribution of the inverse-Compton intensity, the isotropic template can soak up part of the error, and the isotropic background would come out biased. The authors therefore add two models with more freedom. Model B has a separate, electron-only source population near the Galactic center that produces most of the inverse-Compton emission (plus a local source of soft electrons for the electron spectrum measured at Earth below 20 GV). Model C makes the diffusion coefficient and the re-acceleration strength depend on Galactocentric radius and height, and concentrates the sources more toward the center than the pulsar distribution. All three include re-acceleration; A is the baseline but is not treated as preferred.

question: Kim, Lee and Shin proposed in 2008 a renormalizable model of singlet fermionic dark matter, in which a gauge-singlet Dirac fermion ψ couples to the Standard Model through the mixing of a real singlet scalar with the Higgs boson. For their parameter set with Higgs masses m_h1 = 90 GeV and m_h2 = 500 GeV: which condition do they impose from the LEP2 Higgs searches, for which dark matter masses does the region allowed by the relic abundance satisfy it and why, and what do the direct-detection experiments of that time imply for this LEP2-allowed region?

question: Both Calore, Cholis and Weniger (arXiv:1409.0042v1) and the Fermi-LAT Collaboration (arXiv:1704.03910v2) estimate how well the Galactic diffuse emission is modeled by fitting a dark-matter-like template in control regions along the Galactic plane, away from the Galactic Center. For each paper: at which longitudes is the template placed, and how are the results of these fits turned into a systematic uncertainty for the Galactic Center? For arXiv:1409.0042v1, also give the number of overlapping regions in which the template is fitted (the one centred on the Galactic Center included) and the number that enters the uncertainty estimate.
reference_answer: arXiv:1409.0042v1 (Sec. 4.2): the excess template is moved along the disk in steps of 5° and centered at ℓ = k·5°, k = −14, …, 14, i.e. 29 overlapping regions (28 away from the Galactic Center and the one centred on it) (−20° + k·5° ≤ ℓ ≤ 20° + k·5°, 2° ≤ |b| ≤ 20°) covering |ℓ| ≤ 90°, each fitted with all 60 diffuse-emission models. question: According to arXiv:1503.01773v2, once dark-sector cascades with any combination of hierarchical and degenerate decay steps are allowed, what is the shape of the region of the (m_χ, ⟨σv⟩) plane in which a given Standard Model final state can fit the Galactic Center excess, and by which two scaling relations between ⟨σv⟩ and m_χ is that region bounded?
reference_answer: The best fits fill a triangle in the m_χ–⟨σv⟩ plane. Its two edges are the power laws ⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ and ⟨σv⟩ ∝ m_χ^1.3. (A degenerate step doubles the preferred mass and the cross section together, which gives the linear edge; the steeper edge is the approximate power law that the best fits follow as hierarchical steps are added.)
